summary:
Anambra is a state in south-eastern Nigeria, capital Awka, formed in 1976 and Igbo-majority in population. It sits south of the twelve northern Nigerian states that apply Shari'a criminal law, so the death-penalty provisions those states provide for male sodomy do not reach Anambra. Same-sex sexual activity in Anambra carries the secular statutory maximum of up to 14 years' imprisonment.

Anambra stands under Nigeria's national framework, and the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 is the statute that sets the penalty ceiling in this state. In 2022 a court ruled sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Act unconstitutional and unenforceable in any part of the country; that ruling applies in Anambra as it does elsewhere.

No Anambra-specific arrest pattern, police practice, hate-crime measure or state-level protective legislation appears in the sources. The national assessment of Nigeria carries the enforcement picture for this state, and no region-specific signal was identified beyond the jurisdictional facts above.
tangentialFactors:
Mass arrests at hotel parties and private gatherings have been documented in neighbouring and other Nigerian states rather than in Anambra: more than 100 people were arrested at a hotel party in Asaba, Delta State, in June 2018, and 67 people were arrested in Warri, Delta State, in August 2023. These are counts of people arrested, not per-capita rates, and the sources provide no denominator, so the figures rank jurisdictions by raw count only and do not measure risk relative to Anambra.

Anambra's position in the south-east means the coercive tools documented in the northern Shari'a states, including the death penalty for male sodomy, are absent here, while the federal statutory ceiling of 14 years remains in force. The practical exposure a visitor faces in Anambra therefore turns on discretionary police conduct under the national statute rather than on any harsher local penalty regime.
localsOnly:
Residents of Anambra live under the national Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 and its associated provisions, with no state-level protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity recorded in the sources. The 2022 ruling voiding sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of that Act is available to residents throughout the country, including in Anambra, though no Anambra court's application of it is documented here.

The sources record no Anambra Correctional Service practice, no state custody-placement rule for transgender detainees, and no state medical-care or policing guidance for LGBTQ+ residents. Where those matters are documented in Nigeria, the accounts are national or drawn from other states.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Anambra police have conducted raids, hotel-party arrests or 'look gay' extortion stops is unresolved: no Anambra enforcement incident appears in the inventory, and the absence of one is not evidence that none occurs.

The scope and subsequent treatment of the 2022 constitutional ruling in Anambra is not sourced. Whether Anambra courts have applied it, and whether any state bill on cross-dressing or related conduct has been tabled in the Anambra House of Assembly, is not stated in the available material.

No figure for violence against LGBTQ+ people in Anambra, and no Anambra homicide or assault count for any period, is available in the inventory, so no rate comparison can be made for this state.
